  https://www.codyco.ai/

## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

Forward unanswered calls to an outside service / Connect it to the hotel's PMS / Let an AI answer guests in the hotel's voice / Set which calls go to the desk -- with 'Let an AI answer guests in the hotel's voice' selected, so the belief reads 'Most would let an AI answer guests in the hotel's voice.'

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out, it is the obvious moment to decide whether people who answer can ask for a pilot, and my whole sale runs through a paid pilot at one hotel.
screens.why2: Pilot is my own word and the hint is short, but 'Offer a pilot?' does not say whether it means my paid €3,000 money-back pilot or a free try, so I read it twice.
screens.why3: Whether to offer a pilot is a decision I make myself and already have terms for, so I can answer at once.
screens.why4: All I can do here is press Continue, so the hint's 'Optional' shows that I can skip it, but the screen gives me no clear yes, no, or place to put my pilot's terms.
screens.why5: Pilot is my word and nothing is misstated, but the screen drops what I typed about the paid pilot at one location, up to 8 weeks with the money back, so it reads as generic.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot to the people who answer? Options: Yes, the pilot I described (€3,000 at one hotel, up to 8 weeks, money back) / Yes, but with different terms / No, not in this study. Nothing here changes their answers.

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out to reservation agents, it is obvious why Keel asks how they will be interviewed, and nothing I typed earlier already answered this.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but "this account runs on its own AI" and "Keel's credits" need a second read, and "who should ask" sits oddly with a hint saying people read and tap with no interviewer.
screens.why3: As the founder I know my agents work the phones in German hotels, and I can decide how they should get my questions.
screens.why4: The choice is not a real one on this account: a face is preselected and locked, and it appears to matter little when people simply read and tap, with the AI interviewer available only through credits.
screens.why5: Nothing here rewrites my idea, my hotel-group customers or my words, so the screen still means what I set up.
screens.instead: How should reservation agents answer your questions? (Read and tap: included on this account / Talk to the AI interviewer: needs Keel credits)

screens.why1: Having written the study and picked who asks the questions, it is obvious that I now choose how the reservation agents will answer before I send it.
screens.why2: The choice is clear on first read, but the line "Every answer in a quiet room. More than 9 in 10 where it is loud" reads as a fragment and I had to reread it to see it means how many spoken answers get understood.
screens.why3: I know how my agents and directors work, on shift at a desk or in a central office with calls coming in, so I can judge which format suits them.
screens.why4: AI video, text only and letting them choose are complete and distinct, the credits cost is flagged where it applies, and no option is missing for me.
screens.why5: My pick of text only is shown as I made it, and nothing on the screen changes what I typed about my idea.
screens.instead: How should they answer? AI interviewer: a face on video asks each question aloud and they talk, type or tap; spoken answers are understood every time in a quiet room and more than 9 in 10 times somewhere loud (needs Keel's credits). Text only: they read each question and tap or type. Let them choose: they pick one when they open the link (needs Keel's credits).

screens.why1: After choosing how they answer, the last thing before the study goes out is who receives it, so the question is obvious here.
screens.why2: The three options are plain to me on first read, though 'the Contacts page' assumes I know Keel's screen, and I do by this point of the flow.
screens.why3: I know whether I have named reservation agents from the hotel groups we work with or need to find or post for them, so I can answer from my own situation.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel search and an open group link are distinct and cover how I would reach agents, and my own pick of named people is there.
screens.why5: The screen is about distribution only and changes nothing I typed about the idea, the reservation agents or the pilot.

screens.why1: As the first question on a link I did not ask for, it is obvious why they check that I work at the kind of place the study is about.
screens.why2: I understand it at once, but I would say Reservierungszentrale or central reservations, and the tacked-on 'or call center' makes me wonder for a second whether our office counts.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I work for and that we run a central reservations office in Munich, so I can answer without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly for a gate, they do not overlap, and the guidelines give a gate no escape.
screens.why5: No product leaks to me, but the question reads like the founder's segment line copied word for word rather than something a person in my office would ask.
screens.why6: It is one question with a short yes-or-no that I can hold after one hearing, but at 19 words with 'hotel group in Germany' and 'central reservations office or call center' it is a slight mouthful, right at the limit.
screens.instead: Do you take booking calls at a hotel group's central reservations office in Germany? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: After asking where I work, it makes sense to check that I had calls this week, but on a reservations desk calls come in all shift, every shift, so it feels like a question with only one answer.
screens.why2: "Booking call" and "shift" are the words I use every day, and I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether I worked this week and took booking calls.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but "I can't recall one particular booking call" doesn't fit a question about whether any call came in, and "I'd rather not say" is pointless on something this harmless.
screens.why5: It stays with booking calls on my shift in the last 7 days, and nothing about a product or the founder's plan reaches me.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is one short question ending in "Yes or no", which I can answer after hearing it once.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you take a booking call on your shift? Yes / No (no escape chip)

screens.why1: After being asked whether I work in a reservations office and took booking calls, it makes sense to be shown the idea and told this is the part about it.
screens.why2: Forwarded calls, payment, confirmed booking, booking system and OPERA Cloud are all everyday words at my desk, so I understand it on first reading, though "in the hotel's voice" is slightly vague.
screens.why3: It describes calls we miss, bookings we enter in OPERA and calls handed to our desk, all things I handle on a shift and can picture.
screens.why4: The card shows no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: It is an idea card shown on purpose, set out plainly as what it is and what its builders believe, and nothing leaks in words meant for someone other than me.
screens.why6: The short sentences say well, but "booking system: OPERA Cloud" has a colon that only the eye reads and the spoken version runs to eight sentences with no how-it-works break, a lot to hold in one hearing.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco. Calls nobody picks up are forwarded to it, and it answers in the hotel's voice, answers the guest's questions and takes the payment. It writes the confirmed booking straight into OPERA Cloud and hands calls to your desk by rules you set. The people building it believe it would turn every guest who calls into a booking.

screens.why1: After the idea card it makes sense to ask whether it would fit my work, but the last booking call I took was one I answered, so jumping from there to unanswered calls is abrupt.
screens.why2: Forwarding and unanswered calls are everyday words at my desk, but I need a second read to work out how "could you have" applies to one call and several unanswered ones, and whether it means me or our phone system.
screens.why3: I know how to transfer a call, but overflow and after-hours routing in our central office is set by IT or the team lead, so I would partly be guessing.
screens.why4: The scale mixes ease and extent, so "Yes, easily" and "Yes, mostly" do not sit on one line, and "mostly" overlaps with "Only sometimes", though "I can't tell" fits as the escape.
screens.why5: "Imagine Codyco" tells me only a name, so the question has to carry the idea by itself and it reaches me as a question about call forwarding rather than whether the idea fits my work.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is short and has one question, and four brief options and the escape are easy to hold after one hearing.
screens.instead: Think of the last booking call on your shift that nobody answered. Could that call have been forwarded to another number? Yes, without any trouble; Yes, but with some setup; No, our phone system doesn't allow it; or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: After the idea card and a question about my last booking call, it makes sense to ask whether this thing would have helped on that call.
screens.why2: "Make it go better" is loose, because "it" has to refer back to my last booking call, and that call was answered, so I would need a second to work out what "it" means.
screens.why3: I know my calls and my shift, but the card only says "Imagine Codyco", so I would be partly guessing at what it does and how it would have changed that call.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover the range in the words I would use, and "I can't tell" is the honest way out when I know so little about it.
screens.why5: The name Codyco reaches me as an unexplained brand with nothing on the card saying what it does, so what the founder means has thinned out on this screen, though no internal terms leak to me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options I can hold after one hearing and a single escape said last, though the "it" is no clearer aloud than on the screen.
screens.instead: Would Codyco have made your last booking call go better, or not? A lot better; A little better; No difference; Worse; or I can't tell.

screens.why1: After the idea and the question about whether it would have helped, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually send our unanswered calls there.
screens.why2: Forwarding unanswered booking calls is everyday language on my desk, and I understand the question on first hearing.
screens.why3: I can say whether I'd want it, but call forwarding in our central office is set by the team lead or IT, so I'd partly be guessing what I would really do.
screens.why4: "Only if it only takes the calls nobody picks up" is odd because the question already covers only unanswered calls, so it nearly repeats "Yes", though the other options and "I can't tell" fit.
screens.why5: It only uses the name and forwarding idea from the card I've already seen, and it doesn't reveal any plan or use any label for people like me.
screens.why6: It is short and clearly one question, but the "only if it only" option is a mouthful that I'd need to hear twice.
screens.instead: Codyco means forwarding your unanswered booking calls to Codyco. Would you do that, or not? Yes; Only for after-hours and peak-time calls; Probably not; or No. Or say I can't tell.
